concepts.title: G.S. Ghurye: Indology and the Study of Caste

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'G.S. Ghurye: Indology and the Study of Caste' refers to.
questions.a: G.S. Ghurye, father of Indian sociology, drew on Sanskritic textual sources -- the Indological approach -- to study Indian society, and his classic work on caste identified six features: segmental division, hierarchy, restrictions on feeding and social intercourse, civil and religious disabilities, lack of unrestricted choice of occupation, and endogamy.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'G.S. Ghurye: Indology and the Study of Caste'.
questions.a: Read the classics, count the features -- Ghurye systematised caste as six linked restrictions rooted in Brahmanical texts.

concepts.title: D.P. Mukerji and the Tradition-Directed Path

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'D.P. Mukerji and the Tradition-Directed Path' refers to.
questions.a: D.P. Mukerji argued Indian sociology must be grounded in the living traditions of Indian society and in proficiency with Indian languages, not merely in western concepts. Tradition, for him, was not dead custom but a dynamic inheritance; the sociologist's task was to study how tradition adapts and changes under modern forces.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'D.P. Mukerji and the Tradition-Directed Path'.
questions.a: Know your own traditions and languages before theorising India -- sociology here must grow from native ground.

concepts.title: A.R. Desai and the Marxist Approach; M.N. Srinivas and Sanskritisation

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'A.R. Desai and the Marxist Approach; M.N. Srinivas and Sanskritisation' refers to.
questions.a: Two further currents shaped Indian sociology. A.R. Desai applied a Marxist framework, reading Indian history and nationalism in terms of economic structures and class forces. M.N. Srinivas, through intensive fieldwork, gave sociology concepts from within: sanskritisation -- lower groups adopting customs of higher groups -- and westernisation, plus the village study tradition.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'A.R. Desai and the Marxist Approach; M.N. Srinivas and Sanskritisation'.
questions.a: Class analysis from above, village fieldwork from within -- Desai and Srinivas set the poles of Indian sociological debate.
